approved: Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would make permanent the structure and duties of Jobs and Skills Australia, a body that gives independent advice to the government.
It would create a Commissioner and up to two Deputy Commissioners to lead the agency, and let the Minister set up an advisory board with representatives from states, unions, employers and others.
The Minister must order a review of the agency within two years of the changes starting, and table the review in Parliament.
Renames the head of the agency from Director to Commissioner.
Adds functions including advising on insecure work, analysing skills gaps, and publishing an annual work plan.
Requires a parliamentary review within two years of commencement.
Jobs and Skills Australia, the Minister, the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, and stakeholders in vocational education, training and the labour market.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2023-05-11.4.2) to agree with the main idea of the bill. In other words, they voted to read it for a second time. This means that they can now consider it in greater detail. ### What does this bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2223a/23bd071a) summary: * *The [Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6999) (the Bill) amends the Jobs and Skills Australia Act 2022 (the JSA Act) to provide for governance arrangements and functions of Jobs and Skills Australia (JSA).* * *The JSA Act established JSA as a statutory body within the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) and set out its interim functions and staffing arrangements, including establishing a JSA Director to commence JSA’s work.* * *This Bill establishes the permanent arrangements for JSA, following consultation.* * *The Bill amends the JSA Act to establish the role of the JSA Commissioner and JSA Deputy Commissioners, establish a Ministerial Advisory Board, and expand the functions of JSA. It also sets out transparency measures in relation to JSA’s work plan and reporting and provides for a review of the operation of the JSA Act in 2 years.*

The government introduced the Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023 to establish Jobs and Skills Australia as a permanent, independent statutory body with tripartite governance—including union, employer and state/territory representation—to provide labour market and skills advice. The bill expands its functions to include workforce forecasting, regional analysis, studies on insecure work and disadvantage, and skills needs related to migration, clean energy and foundation skills, alongside existing investments such as $6.3 billion for vocational education in 2022-23, 480,000 fee-free TAFE places, and 10,000 New Energy Apprenticeships.

The coalition supported the Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023 but will move amendments to remove mandated union representation on its ministerial advisory board, instead requiring small-business and rural/regional representatives and one member from each state and territory. They also propose an independent review within 12 months rather than two years, and will oppose the bill if the amendments are not supported, arguing the agency is not independent and the government is prioritising "jobs for mates" over merit.

The coalition argued the Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023 would give unions up to 50% representation on the ministerial advisory board despite only 12.5% of employees being union members, and proposed amendments to remove three union seats, add small‑business and rural/regional/remote representatives, and mandate a review within 12 months.

The Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023 was argued to permanently establish Jobs and Skills Australia to address Australia’s skills crisis, citing the second-highest labour supply shortage among OECD countries, 65% employer recruitment difficulty (80% in construction), and a commitment to 180,000 fee-free TAFE places in 2023, growing to 480,000 over five years, with $6.3 billion for VET and a tripling of the bulk-billing incentive.

The speaker argued that the Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023 addresses a skills shortage caused by nine years of Liberal government neglect, which left 85,000 fewer apprenticeships than in 2013. The bill establishes Jobs and Skills Australia as a permanent statutory body with tripartite governance to provide independent advice on labour market needs, including a national study on adult literacy, numeracy, and digital literacy, and is backed by $6.3 billion for vocational education and training and fee-free TAFE places.
